newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus finance minister sees stronger 1997 growth.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus finance minister sees stronger 1997 growth.

text.p: Cyprus's gross domestic product is expected to grow by three percent in 1997 compared with a provisional two percent rise in 1996, Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou said on Monday.

Speaking after a meeting with economic departmental heads, Christodoulou reaffirmed that the island would deregulate capital flows and interest rate ceilings by early next year, when Cyprus is due to start accession negotiations with the European Union.

"One year ago we announced that the liberalisation of the sector, and especially that of interest rates and capital, would take place by the start of the accession negotiations, in March or April of 1998. There has been no issue for suspending or freezing this (intention)," Christodoulou said.

A nine percent interest rate cap has been in force since 1944, imposed by the former British colonial administration to curb usury, limiting the use of interest rates as an instrument of credit policy.
Exchange control restrictions are still in force, but are gradually being eased.

The government and the central bank expect a modest revival in economic activity this year after a slowdown in 1996 which saw real gross domestic product expand by 2.0 percent after a rise of 6.0 percent in 1995.

A contraction in tourist arrivals by seven percent in 1996, spurred by deaths on the ceasefire line dividing Greek and Turkish communities, was seen as one of the main reasons for the decline in growth.

It also underlined the over-reliance Cyprus has on tourism, which represents a fifth of the eastern Mediterranean island's GDP. Christodoulou said tourist arrivals in 1997 are one percent up compared to last year.
The economy was healthy but needed to switch from traditional sectors to the emerging areas of education, health and consultative services.

"It should branch out into new promising sectors, like that of education, heath, consultative and professional services along with the development of new industry which has a future and which will make use of our comparative advantages, especially that of our people," he said.
Christodoulou said other countries had placed emphasis on enacting legislation providing university-level education for foreigners.
"We should insist on our goals of steady development, for a reduction in consumer expenditure and to promote sectors which will give new potential," he said.
